text: A new, golden image arrives, but a successful build is not yet a trusted production release. BlueOps turns that gap into a controlled journey. Build a shared base, prove each workload, then earn the right to promote. The journey starts with a GovTech GCC golden Amazon Linux 2023 image, a baseline with hardening and some operations agents. An EventBridge discovery signal is part of the proposed design. Record the immutable source identity before the factory moves. ImageBuilder combines that approved source with approved GCC agent packages and a selected CIS hardening profile. The product is hardened base OS. Package only means no production manager registration baked into the image. Selected controls do not mean full CIS compliance or complete security scan acceptance. Free child families derive directly from that base, GitLab, MongoDB, and CloudOS ECS Worker. The shared base stays in development. GitLab carries its own required runtime. MongoDB is non-container by default. GitLab plus Nextflow is an optional extension, not a fourth core family. Now the test floor. Every result must identify the exact candidate. Private connectivity, no public IP, SSM readback, packages, configuration, and provenance all matter. For GitLab, demand healthy service. Representative clone and push, create, read, update, and delete, persistence, and reboot proof. Current private runtime checks cover cold boot and reboot. They do not by themselves prove authenticated repository workflows or a production cutover. MongoDB needs a running process, create, read, update, and delete, and backup restore smoke. Those standalone checks do not prove a healthy replica set. A proposed higher confidence cluster gate would test replication and recovery. Until it passes, cluster readiness remains unknown. CloudOS ECS Worker must place tasks on the exact candidate. Zero-place tasks is a failure, even when the image build is green. Our proposed demo suite adds mock workloads, service-to-service network flows, and scoped parameter store reads through authorized IAM. These are simulated tests, not live evidence. Phase A is a controlled release. Development proof comes first. Only validated child images move toward production acceptance. Verify encryption, AMI launch access, and usable backing snapshots and KMS access. A policy observation alone does not prove a successful private launch. Test the exact image consumed in production with that environment's own agent configuration. Development success cannot stand in for production runtime acceptance. The Ops Engineer reviews the evidence and gives explicit approval for this rollout. Build success, validation, and human approval are separate states. Phase B is a future operating policy. Candidates could build and validate weekly. The proposed promotion window is the first Saturday night each month. Promotion without per-release ops approval becomes possible only after management, security, and change governance approve that policy and its conditions. The current repository does not establish unattended monthly production rollout. A critical vulnerability can instead trigger an urgent ops-approved release. A failed or unknown check, missing approval or policy, missing access, or an unhealthy production cannery closes the gate. Nothing advances on an assumption. Keep the prior known good release and a tested data recovery path. Read back the rollout result. If the canary fails, stop and use the approved rollback plan. A few minutes of downtime may be acceptable if approved. Reversibility and observable acceptance matter more than a green build badge. Build once. Validate every workload. Promote only what is proven.
